title: A taste of next week
hook: the Shabbat afternoon reading begins next week's portion

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musaf, the extra prayer for an extra day. Your line was an extra portion. What extra good thing did you add? Today, Shabbat afternoon, when the Torah comes out one more time. Day six hundred twenty-two.

You know the trick TV shows use at the end of an episode. A few seconds of next week's story. Just enough so you come back. Shabbat afternoon has its own version. The morning's long reading is done, lunch has been eaten, maybe a nap was taken. Then, late in the day, at the afternoon service, the scroll comes out of the ark again. But it isn't rolled back to this week's portion. It's rolled forward. Three people are called up, and the congregation hears the opening of next week's portion. A preview.
screen: `A FEW SECONDS OF NEXT WEEK.` → `THE SCROLL COMES OUT AGAIN.` → `ROLLED FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Where does this come from? The Talmud, in tractate Bava Kamma, lists ten enactments it credits to Ezra the scribe, and reading the Torah at Shabbat afternoon prayer is one of them. The reason it gives is lovely and practical: for the shopkeepers. As the classic commentator Rashi explains, these were people too busy all week to hear Torah on Monday and Thursday. Wait, Monday and Thursday? Yes. That same short section, the opening of the coming week's portion, is read again on Monday and Thursday mornings. So the week has a rhythm. Saturday afternoon, a taste. Monday, again. Thursday, again. And then, next Saturday morning, the whole portion. The Talmud traces the Monday and Thursday readings to a verse from Exodus. Right after crossing the sea, the people "went three days in the wilderness, and found no water," and when they finally found some, it was bitter. The rabbis read water as Torah. Three days without it is too long. So the Torah is never more than three days away. In many communities, the afternoon service says a verse about timing just before the scroll comes out. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 69: "But as for me, let my prayer be unto Thee, O LORD, in an acceptable time." Late Shabbat afternoon is treated as one of those times. Notice what that does. Shabbat is about stopping, but it also leans forward. Even on the day of rest, you're handed a little of what's coming. You start next week before this week ends.
screen: `EZRA: FOR THE SHOPKEEPERS.` · `SATURDAY, MONDAY, THURSDAY.` · `NEVER THREE DAYS WITHOUT WATER.` · `IN AN ACCEPTABLE TIME.` · then, large: `A TASTE OF NEXT WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look ahead to next week's portion. If you can, find out its name and read its first few verses. If not, take a minute now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the week ahead, not as a list of tasks, but as a story about to begin. What's the first scene? What one thing are you looking forward to? Let yourself have a taste of it now, without worrying. The bell holds the time.
A taste of next week. The Shabbat afternoon reading, which opens the coming week's portion and comes back on Monday and Thursday.
screen: `A TASTE OF NEXT WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a taste of next week. Today, do one small thing that starts something you're looking forward to. Day six hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: At Shabbat Mincha the Torah is taken out and three people are called up for the opening section of the next week's portion; the same section is read on Monday and Thursday mornings, before the full portion is read the following Shabbat.

trapdoor: what you thought: one more reading to fill the afternoon.
what it means: a preview that ties the weeks together, so Torah is never three days away.
what a scholar hears: Bava Kamma 82a credits Ezra with the Shabbat Mincha reading and ties Monday and Thursday to Exodus 15:22.

notes: Exodus 15:22 and Psalm 69:14 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Bava Kamma 82a: Ezra's enactments include Shabbat Mincha reading 'because of the shopkeepers' (yoshvei keranot); Monday/Thursday readings attributed there to the prophets among them / Moses, with Ezra adding the number of readers. Simplified; confirm.
Psalm 69:14 is said at Shabbat Mincha in Ashkenazi practice before the Torah reading; customs vary. Teach now says 'in many communities'.
The shopkeepers 'too busy all week to hear Torah on Monday and Thursday' is Rashi's explanation of yoshvei keranot; now attributed to Rashi.
Exodus 15:22–23: three days without water, then bitter water at Marah; earlier 'they grew bitter' corrected to the water being bitter.
